params.text:
In 1900, three lighthouse keepers
vanished from the Flannan Isles.

A remote archipelago
in the Outer Hebrides of Scotland.

The lighthouse stood on Eilean Mòr —
the largest of the group.

On December 15th, a passing ship
noticed the light was dark.

No flag was flying.
No supplies had been landed for weeks.

When a relief vessel finally arrived
on December 26th, the lighthouse was silent.

The door was unlocked.
The beds were unmade.
A meal sat half-eaten on the table.

But the three keepers —
James Ducat, Thomas Marshall,
and Donald MacArthur — were gone.

The lighthouse log recorded
a violent storm on the 12th and 13th of December.

The entries grew increasingly frantic.
Then, on the 14th,
the final entry read:

"Storm ended, sea calm.
God is over all."

But there was no storm recorded
by weather stations on the mainland.

No ship reported bad weather
in the area that week.

Some say the keepers disappeared
during a real storm —
one never recorded.

Others believe a fight
broke out between them.

A popular theory claims one keeper
go mad and killed the others.

The logbook tells a darker story:
entries about cursing, prayers,
and a final supper.

But the log was never found.
Only fragments survive.

Whatever happened on that remote rock,
the sea kept its secret.

The Flannan Isles lighthouse was automated
in 1971. No keeper has lived there since.

To this day, the disappearance remains
one of Britain's most enduring mysteries.
